work.title: String Quartet No. 14 in C♯ minor
work.movement: I–VII. Complete quartet — seven linked movements in one archival file
work.version.value: Original quartet scoring; all seven numbered movements presented in a single joined transfer.
work.version.note: The item explicitly presents the complete work in one file. This establishes the intended movement coverage, not a bar-by-bar audit: the performing edition, cuts, repeat observance and any material removed at side joins remain unknown. The public-domain score used for commentary is not identified as the players’ edition.
performers.value: [{"name":"Léner String Quartet","role":"string quartet"},{"name":"Jenö Léner","role":"first violin"},{"name":"Joszef Smilovits","role":"second violin"},{"name":"Sándor Roth","role":"viola"},{"name":"Imre Hartman","role":"cello"}]
performers.note: The item assigns first and second violin; DAHR confirms the four names and instruments. The photographed label uses the spellings Lener, Smilovits, Roth and Hartmann.
session.date.note: These are four session dates for the issued masters, not one continuous performance. AX300–301: 11 February; AX323–328: 21 February; AX332: 22 February; issued AX302 take 4: 25 August. DAHR marks some unissued AX302 dates unconfirmed; that qualification is not attached to its issued take-4 row. The item’s short February/August summary must not erase the two additional February dates in its own side list.
session.place.value: Columbia’s Petty France Studios, London, England
session.place.note: The studio is named by the transfer author on the Archive item. The consulted individual DAHR master records independently give London, not the studio.
carrier.label.note: The item explicitly says the transfer derives from the British issue. The photographed L1581 label reads Columbia Graphophone Co. Limited, London and Made in England.
carrier.catalogue.value: Columbia (UK) L1581–L1585; corresponding US issue 67021-D–67025-D, Masterworks Set 6
carrier.catalogue.note: Five double-sided 12-inch discs. The Archive description dates both British and US publication to November 1924. DAHR identifies the set as M-6 but notes that pre-CBS pressings may lack the M prefix; M-6 is therefore a discographic identifier, not a claim about the original album’s typography.
carrier.matrixTakeSides.value: ["Side 1: AX300-1 — I, first part — 11 February 1924","Side 2: AX301-1 — I, second part — 11 February 1924","Side 3: AX302-4 — II and III — 25 August 1924","Side 4: AX323-3 — IV, first part — 21 February 1924","Side 5: AX324-2 — IV, second part — 21 February 1924","Side 6: AX325-2 — IV, third part — 21 February 1924","Side 7: AX326-1 — IV, fourth part; V, first part — 21 February 1924","Side 8: AX327-2 — V, second part — 21 February 1924","Side 9: AX328-2 — VI; VII, first part — 21 February 1924","Final side: AX332-2 — VII, second part — 22 February 1924"]
carrier.matrixTakeSides.note: All ten matrix/take pairs and session dates agree with the DAHR set listing. Movement-to-side allocation comes from the Archive description, with AX301, AX302 and AX332 individually corroborated by DAHR part titles. The item calls the last entry ‘Side 19’; it is retained here as ‘Final side’, not treated as evidence of nineteen sides. The label photograph establishes AX300 and L1581 but does not make the take suffix legible. No physical run-out inspection or digital join-to-matrix alignment has been made.
transfer.credits.note: The description says ‘My transfer’ and identifies the British source discs, but does not name the transfer engineer. The uploader account and shellackophile-recordings collection are not expanded into a personal mastering credit.
transfer.date.note: 27 February 2022 is the item’s added/public date and a digital-file timestamp, not an established date of the analogue transfer.
transfer.processing.value: Ten acoustic-era disc sides joined into one file; Internet Archive VBR MP3 access derivative of an uploaded FLAC.
transfer.processing.note: The item describes the acoustic-era recording and continuous presentation; its file list names the FLAC parent of the selected MP3. The photographed label specifies ‘Speed 80’, not a demonstrated playback speed of this transfer. Stylus, equalisation, de-clicking, noise reduction, join edits, speed adjustment and absolute pitch calibration are unestablished. No tuning value is inferred from automatic key estimates, and no portamento or tempo habit is asserted as an audited feature of this performance.
digital.format: Internet Archive VBR MP3 derivative (listed average 105 kbps), parent L1581-5 Beethoven Quartet op131.flac
rights.composition.value: Underlying composition and the nineteenth-century Breitkopf & Härtel score are public domain.
rights.composition.note: Op. 131 dates from 1826 and was published after Beethoven’s death in 1827. IMSLP identifies the consulted engraving as the 1863 collected edition, plate B.50, and marks it Public Domain. This is not clearance of any unidentified later performing edition.
rights.recording.value: United States public-domain basis: first published in 1924, before the project’s 1926 cutoff.
rights.recording.note: The transfer author expressly dates Columbia L1581–L1585 and US 67021-D–67025-D/Set 6 to November 1924; DAHR corroborates their identity with the 1924 masters, not independently the November publication month. Under the Copyright Office’s stated 95-plus-5-year term for recordings first published in 1923–1946, a 1924 publication has exhausted that term. The Archive metadata supplies no separate Creative Commons recording licence. Admission rests on the historical recording’s US term, not Beethoven’s death, the upload date, an uploader licence or a blanket worldwide clearance. No separate restoration rights claim was identified in the consulted item.

work.movement: III. Molto adagio (Heiliger Dankgesang); the source’s III–IV combined title is disputed
work.version.value: Original quartet scoring; movement III. The Archive’s combined III–IV designation is disputed.
work.version.note: The exact selected 1092.62-second MP3 is retained without truncation or substitution. Its analysed structure supports the five alternating spans of III, at approximately 0, 214, 340, 558 and 686 seconds, followed by slow music through the endpoint. The required report does not establish an A-major march or the IV–V link. Supplementary upper-band inspection finds an F-centred ending; verifier VerH independently checked the selected file’s final37.6s against the score and also found the F ending of III, not IV’s dominant recitative. These are score/audio-feature correspondences, not an aural or complete bar-aligned certification. No IV boundary or IV listening prose is invented. Performing edition, cuts, repeat observance and the completeness of the final played release remain unestablished.

The side-2 FLAC carries ‘Processed by SoX’; the item’s final segmentation is 7.434–1100.006 seconds of that side capture for III–IV. That is a digital cut range, not score alignment. rights.composition.note: The quartet was composed in 1825; Beethoven died in 1827. The consulted Beethovens Werke engraving, plate B.51, is catalogued as the 1863 edition and Public Domain. This does not clear an unidentified later performing edition or the sleeve author’s prose.
rights.recording.value: Territorial EU public-domain basis only: the recording was published before 1963; US status is not established.
rights.recording.note: The admitted basis is eu-published-before-1963, using the Archive’s 1952 catalogue date for this identified London LLP318 issue. The printed sleeve carries a 1951 copyright notice, corroborating an early-1950s package but not independently establishing the first publication year of the sound recording. A recording published by 1952 had exhausted the ordinary EU 50-year phonogram term before 1 November 2013; the 2011 extension applies to recordings still protected on that date. This is territorial, not a Creative Commons grant or worldwide clearance. The US 1947–1956 term is longer, and no US public-domain claim is made. The Archive item supplies no separate recording licence; availability online and Beethoven’s public-domain composition are not the admission basis.

performers.note: The Archive description, selected file’s artist tag and Bloesch’s discography agree. Bloesch’s session list identifies a Bechstein piano; no instrument serial number is established.
session.date.note: The Op. 57 description specifies 11.IV.1933, corroborated by the discography and reissue documentation. The Archive item’s general date of 1932 covers the compilation and is not this sonata’s session date. The embedded date tag 2001 is not treated as a session or transfer date.
session.place.value: Abbey Road Studios, Studio No. 3, London, England
session.place.note: Bloesch’s chronological session list gives Studio No. 3 and a Bechstein piano; the alphabetical work entry gives Abbey Road Studios, London.
carrier.label.note: The original commercial issue was His Master’s Voice. The label of the physical carrier or later reissue actually used to make this MP3 is not identified; original-issue information is not substituted for transfer provenance.
carrier.catalogue.note: Bloesch identifies the original complete-sonata issue as HMV DB 2215–2217 in Beethoven Sonata Society Volume 5, part of set DB 2211–2217. The transferred pressing or reissue catalogue number is unknown. The embedded portrait contains no readable carrier identification.
carrier.matrixTakeSides.note: Original session documentation assigns movement I to two sides, 2B 6605 and 2B 6606, with takes 2 listed as the issued masters; the catalogue lists 2B 6605II and 2B 6606II. These identify the historical issued recording, not an independently verified take selection or side-join position in the selected MP3.
transfer.credits.note: No transfer or restoration engineer is credited for this file. The Archive uploader recordplayer78 is not equated with an engineer or owner. Andrew Rose’s credit on the separately consulted Pristine reissue is not transferred to this MP3; no upstream link to that reissue is established.
transfer.date.note: The Archive added/public date is 27 March 2020. The embedded date tag is 2001, without an identified release or transfer to which it refers. Neither date establishes when the analogue source was transferred or restored.
transfer.processing.value: The MP3’s encoder tag states ‘Audiograbber 1.83.01, LAME dll 3.99, 256 Kbit/s, Joint Stereo, Normal quality’.
transfer.processing.note: Inspection of the downloaded selected stream found MP3 audio at 44,100 Hz, two channels and 256,000 bit/s, plus an attached JPEG portrait. Two-channel encoding is not evidence of an original stereo session. Analogue transfer equipment, equalisation, noise reduction, pitch/speed correction, restoration and edit history remain unknown. Archive calls the file ‘VBR MP3’; that repository format label is distinct from the inspected stream and encoder tag.
digital.format: MP3; inspected audio 256 kb/s, 44.1 kHz, two channels; Archive format label VBR MP3
rights.composition.value: The underlying Beethoven composition is public domain under the ordinary EU life-plus-70 term.
rights.composition.note: Beethoven died in 1827. The cited original score contains the historical composition; no unidentified modern performing edition is cleared by this term calculation. Composition rights are separate from the rights in Schnabel’s recording.
rights.recording.value: Rule 3 — territorial EU public domain: original sound recording first published in 1934.
rights.recording.note: The Public Domain Project release-set catalogue explicitly gives 1934 as the first release of HMV DB 2211–2217; Bloesch identifies Op. 57 within that issue as DB 2215–2217, matrices 2B 6605–6610. Publication is thus documented separately from the 11 April 1933 session. Under the programme’s territorial EU rule, the earlier 50-year term had expired before the 2013 extension. US status is not established and no worldwide clearance is claimed. The Archive’s Public Domain Mark is an assertion, not an ownership release; the Public Domain Project’s worldwide/US expiry table is not relied upon. No CC licence or independently established additional rights in an unidentified modern transfer are asserted.

title: Flute Concerto in G major, Wq 169 / H 445
work.title: Flute Concerto in G major
work.version.value: Flute version of the concerto; complete finale only
work.version.note: Only movement III is hosted in this package. Set metadata records part 3 of 3, not possession of the preceding Allegro di molto and Largo. The 1755 date belongs to the original organ concerto Wq 34; the flute adaptation is later and cannot be assigned a precise year. The working manuscript is dated between 1755 and 1768 by Kuijken. The recording’s performing edition, any restored missing bar and the details of a cadenza are unestablished. The modern critical performing parts clarify the manuscript’s shorthand: flute participates in the opening and closing tutti, so a blank flute staff does not establish a rest. These parts are consulted as a reference, not attributed to the 2008 performance or claimed to be public domain. The score-derived orchestra display uses passage overviews rather than aligned entries; the cello desk represents written basso, not a verified allocation of bass instruments.
performers.note: Both sources name the soloist and ensemble. The opened programme does not identify a conductor for this concerto or its continuo player. Credits for soloists in the adjacent Brandenburg concertos have not been transferred to this track. Exact string numbers, keyboard type, double-bass participation and tuning are unestablished.
session.date.note: Commons gives February 2008 and the upstream Music of the Bach Family programme gives 10 and 17 February. The source does not identify which concert supplies this performance or whether material was combined. The directory’s 7 April 2008 file timestamps and Commons’ 23 November 2008 upload are not session dates. MAR-08 is a repository folder name, not proof of a March performance.
session.place.note: The opened recording page, concert programme and notes do not identify the recording venue. The orchestra’s usual location does not establish this session’s place.

carrier.catalogue.note: No commercial catalogue number is documented. The repository filename 6_CPE_Bach_Concerto_Gmaj_Presto.ogg identifies a digital item, not a record catalogue.

work.version.value: Original orchestral work; exact performing edition unestablished
work.version.note: The sources identify the work and movement, but not the parts or revision used in October 1951. The original Fromont/Kalmus and 1930 Jobert full scores were viewed. Musical annotations use shared principal passages; no claim that Ansermet follows every detail of the revised edition, no cut/repeat-order certification, and no bar-accurate score alignment. Orchestra states are explicitly provisional passage estimates, not audio instrument detection.
performers.note: The instrumental movement has no choral part. No orchestral soloist or complete roster is identified or inferred. The unresolved Sirènes chorus does not enter this movement.
session.date.note: Month and year are corroborated. Stuart’s [a] Nocturnes has no exact day: the 10th and 12th in the shared session heading refer to other works. The 1951 session must not be described as a 1951 publication.
session.place.note: Venue is independently supplied by the session discography and the matching London CD catalogue record.
carrier.label.note: Original British LP label; London LL 530 is the separately dated June 1952 issue in Stuart.
carrier.catalogue.note: First British issue March 1952. Side A contains the three Nocturnes; side B Ravel’s Rapsodie espagnole. Original label images were not present in the IA item, so the date relies on the discography rather than an inspected LP label.
carrier.matrixTakeSides.value: Side A; suite master series SAR587–SAR592
carrier.matrixTakeSides.note: IA identifies the side and track order; Stuart assigns SAR587–92 to Nocturnes as a whole. No individual movement matrix, LP runout, take number or pressing identification is established, and none is extrapolated from the six-number series.
transfer.credits.note: No digital-transfer engineer is credited. IA account identity is not a transfer credit. Victor Olof (producer) and Gil Went (engineer) are documented for the original Decca session, not for this digital transfer.
transfer.date.note: The item was uploaded/published on IA on 26 December 2021. That is not evidence for when the physical record was transferred.
transfer.processing.note: Original FLAC and derived VBR MP3 are listed, but playback equipment, equalisation, de-clicking, noise reduction, pitch correction and intervening edits are undocumented. No listening or processing-quality claim is made.
digital.format: Internet Archive VBR MP3 derivative of the item’s original FLAC; item identifies a transfer from Decca LXT 2637
rights.composition.value: Public-domain underlying composition under ordinary life-plus-70 terms
rights.composition.note: Debussy died in 1918; the original score was published in 1900–01. Original and 1930 score pages were consulted as historical score evidence. This assessment of the composition is separate from sound-recording rights and does not claim rights in a modern edition, scan or arrangement.
rights.recording.value: Rule 3 territorial basis: EU sound recording first published before 1963; US public-domain status not established
rights.recording.note: LXT 2637 was issued in March 1952, not 1951. Under the ordinary former EU 50-year publication term this predates expiry before the 1 November 2013 extension threshold. This is the project’s territorial pre-1963 basis, not a Creative Commons licence or a worldwide public-domain claim. US status has not been established. IA supplies no open-licence URL; the upload alone does not grant rights.

title: Pomp and Circumstance, Op. 39
work.title: Pomp and Circumstance
work.version.value: Orchestral version
work.version.note: The Elgar Society identifies this as Elgar’s first complete recording of the march, distinguishing it from the severely cut 1914 acoustic version. Complete does not establish that every written repeat was taken. The precise performing edition and organ participation are not established.
performers.note: The label explicitly says conducted by Sir Edward Elgar; the composer credit alone was not used to infer this role.
session.date.note: Independently documented in the Elgar Society recording account and Naxos 8.111022 discography. Internet Archive’s date 1927 concerns the Victor issue, not the recording session. The identifier retains that issue year.
session.place.note: Venue is printed on the disc label; it is not inferred from the orchestra’s Royal Albert Hall name.
carrier.label.note: The label says Orthophonic Recording, identifying the electrical process.
carrier.catalogue.note: Victor 9016 couples Marches Nos. 1 and 2; the January 1927 trade listing identifies the same performers.
carrier.matrixTakeSides.note: The specialist Naxos discography lists matrix CR 336-2 and original British issue HMV D 1102. The transferred pressing’s take suffix is not independently legible. Internet Archive’s matrix 9016A is the issue-side number, and its other ID CR331 is not silently adopted as the master number.
transfer.credits.value: George Blood, L.P.; Phoebe Pugh, transfer
transfer.credits.note: The item identifies the digitisation facility and user_transferred field; these are transfer credits, not original session personnel.
transfer.date.note: The November 2023 upload does not establish the transfer date.
transfer.processing.value: Digitised at 78 rpm; preferred 3.8 mil truncated-conical stylus transfer; equalised with turnover 250 and rolloff 0; MP3 derivative
transfer.processing.note: The original FLAC’s embedded comment identifies the selected stylus and equalisation. The site uses the supplied preferred MP3 without joining or changing the audio.
digital.format: VBR MP3 derived from the Great 78 Project’s original FLAC; decoded duration rounded from cache/analysis/elgar-pomp-circumstance-1-elgar-1927.txt
rights.composition.value: Elgar’s original 1901 march is public domain in ordinary life-plus-70 jurisdictions
rights.composition.note: Elgar died in 1934. This concerns the underlying composition, not an unidentified modern edition.
rights.recording.value: Territorial EU public-domain basis: Victor 9016 announced for publication on 28 January 1927
rights.recording.note: Rule 3. The Talking Machine World, 15 January 1927, p. 131, lists 9016 under the Victor list for 28 January, naming both marches and Elgar with the Royal Albert Hall Orchestra. This is publication evidence, not a session-date substitution; the British first issue may be earlier. Its 50-year term expired before the 2013 extension. US status is not established. The selected Great 78 item, original FLAC and label were checked; no NC licence or separate upstream digital recording is stated. The Naxos booklet is used only as documentary evidence: its commercial restoration is not the selected audio.

session.date.note: 16 January is the documented public concert date. session.place.note: The concert-programme catalogue names the hall and city; Commons uses Musikvereinsaal de Vienne.
carrier.label.note: Commons names only an unspecified audio CD. HMV made the original 78-rpm issue, but the CD label used for this upload has not been identified.
carrier.catalogue.note: The source CD catalogue number is unknown. Pristine documents the historical ten-disc HMV set as DB 8569–8578; that does not identify the carrier transferred for Commons.
carrier.matrixTakeSides.note: Pristine lists the original complete-set matrix series 2VH 7027–7046. The inspected DAHR composer listing did not establish a matrix/take match for this digital source; no exhaustive absence is claimed. Specific takes and a verified movement-to-matrix mapping remain unestablished, so the complete-set series is not presented as a side identification for this file.
transfer.credits.note: No engineer for the source CD or Commons transfer is identified. Gaisberg was the original recording producer and Charlie Gregory the recording engineer, not established digital-transfer credits. Andrew Rose’s named 2013 Pristine transfer is a different reissue and is not the source of this Commons upload.

title: Das Lied von der Erde
work.title: Das Lied von der Erde
work.version.note: The item does not say which score edition the orchestra used or whether any passage was cut. The first edition (Universal Edition, 1912) is the score read for the notes on this page; the 1939 performing materials may differ.
performers.note: The item credits Kerstin Thorborg (alto), Carl Martin Öhmann (tenor) and Carl Schuricht (conductor) for the whole concert, and names the singer on each track; Carl Martin Öhmann does not sing in this song. The Mahler Foundation’s discography lists the same three with the Royal Concertgebouw Orchestra, Amsterdam. The orchestra was not yet styled “Royal” in 1939.
session.date.note: The date is in the item’s title and date field and agrees with the Carl Schuricht article; the Mahler Foundation gives only “October 1939 broadcast concert, live”. It is not the upload date (the item was added on 2 July 2022).
session.place.note: Named in the item title (“Concertgebouw Amsterdam”) and in the Mahler Foundation’s listing of a live Amsterdam concert; “Concertgebouw” names both the orchestra and the hall, and neither source names a room.
carrier.label.note: The item names no label and does not state the medium it was copied from. The Mahler Foundation’s discography records a Bel Age CD made “from acetates” of the broadcast; whether this file derives from that issue is not stated.
carrier.catalogue.note: No catalogue number is given for the source of this file.
carrier.matrixTakeSides.note: No acetate matrix, side or take numbers appear in the sources consulted; this is not a claim that they cannot be recovered.
transfer.credits.note: The item names an uploader account but no transfer or restoration engineer; an uploader is not automatically a transfer engineer.
transfer.date.note: The item’s added and public dates (2 July 2022) are upload dates, not transfer dates.
transfer.processing.value: Internet Archive derivatives of a WAV original: this file is a variable-bit-rate MP3 (170 kbps); FLAC and spectrogram derivatives of the same WAV are also listed.
transfer.processing.note: The item description calls it “a good recording”. It does not describe noise reduction, speed correction or equalisation. The Internet Archive item also carries a separate 15-second clip (track 07, “Zwischenruf 6. Satz at 19 min 30 sec (3x)”) in which the uploader isolated an audience interjection that he places at about 19 min 30 s of this movement; the clip is not part of this recording and the words shouted are the uploader’s uncertain hearing.
digital.format: VBR MP3 (170 kbps) derivative supplied by the Internet Archive; original upload WAV
rights.composition.value: Music by Gustav Mahler (died 1911); words adapted by Mahler from Hans Bethge’s Die chinesische Flöte (Bethge died 1946), itself a paraphrase of Tang-dynasty poems by way of French and German translations. The 1912 first edition is hosted on IMSLP as public domain.
rights.composition.note: A term calculation (life plus 70 years; Bethge’s text has been free in life-plus-70 jurisdictions since 2017), not a clearance of every edition or translation.
rights.recording.value: Treated as public domain in the European Union (territorial): a live broadcast of 5 October 1939 whose related rights, on the sources consulted, had expired before the extended terms applied on 1 November 2013. United States status is not established.
rights.recording.note: Before the 2011 extension, Directive 2006/116/EC gave performers and phonogram producers 50-year terms. For a performance of 1939 the performer’s term ran 50 years from the performance, to 1989, unless a fixation of it in a phonogram was lawfully published or lawfully communicated to the public within that period, which would have started a longer term from that event. The live radio broadcast was a communication of the performance, not of a phonogram fixation, and the sources consulted document no earlier publication of the acetate fixation; the date of its first issue on disc is not given in them, so this is an inference, not a clearance. Directive 2011/77/EU lengthened terms to 70 years only for rights still protected on 1 November 2013 (Article 10(5)), so rights that had already expired were not revived. The item carries a Public Domain Mark 1.0 licence URL, which is the uploader’s statement and not the basis used here.

rights.composition.value: Music by Gustav Mahler (died 1911); words adapted by Mahler from Hans Bethge’s Die chinesische Flöte (Bethge died 1946), itself a paraphrase of Tang-dynasty poems by way of French and German translations. The 1912 first edition is hosted on IMSLP as public domain.
rights.composition.note: A term calculation (life plus 70 years; Bethge’s text has been free in life-plus-70 jurisdictions since 2017), not a clearance of every edition or translation.
rights.recording.value: Treated as public domain in the European Union (territorial): a live broadcast of 5 October 1939 whose related rights, on the sources consulted, had expired before the extended terms applied on 1 November 2013. United States status is not established.
rights.recording.note: Before the 2011 extension, Directive 2006/116/EC gave performers and phonogram producers 50-year terms. For a performance of 1939 the performer’s term ran 50 years from the performance, to 1989, unless a fixation of it in a phonogram was lawfully published or lawfully communicated to the public within that period, which would have started a longer term from that event. The live radio broadcast was a communication of the performance, not of a phonogram fixation, and the sources consulted document no earlier publication of the acetate fixation; the date of its first issue on disc is not given in them, so this is an inference, not a clearance. Directive 2011/77/EU lengthened terms to 70 years only for rights still protected on 1 November 2013 (Article 10(5)), so rights that had already expired were not revived. The item carries a Public Domain Mark 1.0 licence URL, which is the uploader’s statement and not the basis used here.

work.version.note: The source identifies the orchestral song, but not its performing edition or editorial alterations. The listening notes use the low-voice orchestral score, C. F. Kahnt plate 4460, for passage-level scoring; they do not claim this exact printed edition was on the performers’ desks. In this transfer, songs IV–V have late pitch-class profiles about a semitone above the written score and the Fischer-Dieskau transfer. The cause—speed, transposition or other processing—has not been established. No tuning correction or numerical tempo comparison is asserted.
performers.note: The Commons description identifies all three performing credits; the independent catalogue corroborates the pairing.
session.date.note: Commons dates the recording to 1950; the day and month remain unestablished. The earlier RCA release catalogue is not used as a session-date source.
session.place.note: The consulted sources do not identify the recording venue. The orchestra’s home city is not used as proof of the session location.
carrier.label.note: Commons names its source as “CD audio RCA”. This is the identified CD source label, not an assertion about the original session medium.
carrier.catalogue.note: No catalogue number identifying the CD used for the Commons upload is supplied. An independent University of the Arts Helsinki catalogue documents an earlier RCA Victor Red Seal LP, LM 1146, with these performers, coupled with Brahms’s Alto Rhapsody; its catalogue date is 1951 and its descriptive release range is 1951–1953. It identifies an earlier issue, not the CD transferred to Commons.
carrier.matrixTakeSides.note: No matrix, take or original side identification is supplied. The absence of those details is not treated as proof that no historical identifiers exist.
transfer.credits.note: The Commons uploader is not treated as a transfer or mastering engineer. No such credit for this particular CD-to-Ogg transfer is identified.
transfer.date.note: No transfer date is supplied; upload dates and historical recording dates are not substituted for it.
transfer.processing.value: Commons provides an uploaded Ogg Vorbis file and an MP3 access derivative.
transfer.processing.note: The embedded Ogg encoder is Xiph.Org libVorbis I 20100325 (Everywhere). The original session medium, earlier mastering, noise reduction and editing history are unestablished. In this transfer, songs IV–V have late pitch-class profiles about a semitone above the written score and the Fischer-Dieskau transfer. The cause—speed, transposition or other processing—has not been established. No tuning correction or numerical tempo comparison is asserted. The analyzed final-song derivative contains approximately twenty seconds at the analysis floor after the closing decay; this is not treated as sustained orchestral sound.
digital.format: MP3 access derivative supplied by Wikimedia Commons; uploaded source: Ogg Vorbis

rights.composition.note: The catalogue gives Mahler’s dates as 1860–1911 and Rückert’s as 1788–1866. This refers to the historical composition and text, not an unidentified modern performing edition; the catalogue’s inconsistent publication year is not adopted.

work.title: Rückert-Lieder
work.movement: Ich bin der Welt abhanden gekommen — concert-band arrangement
work.version.value: Arrangement for soprano, English horn solo and concert band; arranger not identified
work.version.note: Commons names the Navy Concert Band, a soprano and an English horn but does not name an arranger or edition. Mahler wrote the song for voice with piano or orchestra, so a band performance implies an arrangement. This recording’s chroma estimates read F major, whereas the first-edition orchestral score on IMSLP (22552) is notated in E♭ major; IMSLP lists the song in F major and notes transposed publications. The estimates suggest a possible pitch difference from that edition, but neither the arrangement’s key nor any transposition has been confirmed.

title: Piano Concerto No. 21 in C major, K. 467
work.title: Piano Concerto No. 21 in C major
work.version.note: The exact performing edition is not identified. Bolig explicitly credits Artur Schnabel with the first-movement cadenza; the consulted public-domain score marks the cadenza slot but does not contain his notes. The Archive description says that an earlier file mix-up with K. 595 has been corrected; the current file attribution follows that corrected record, not the superseded review. No bar-by-bar or aural authentication of the transfer has been made.
performers.note: The Archive description, photographed LP sleeve and orchestra discography agree. Bolig and the Schnabel chronology identify a Bechstein piano. The later sleeve uses Sargent’s title Sir; that is not treated as evidence of his title at the 1937 session.
session.date.note: LSO session 0158 distinguishes K. 467, recorded on 12 January, from K. 459, recorded on 9 and 12 January. The date is independently stated in the Archive description and the side-level discographies.
session.place.note: The Archive names Abbey Road Studios; the LSO register, Bolig and Schnabel chronology specify Studio 1. The recording venue is not inferred merely from the orchestra’s name.
carrier.label.value: Angel Records — Great Recordings of the Century
carrier.label.note: This is the documented mono LP used for Bob Varney’s transfer, not the original shellac carrier. The original recording was issued by His Master’s Voice.
carrier.catalogue.note: The photographed sleeve prints COLH 67 and pairs K. 467 under Sargent with K. 595 under Barbirolli. LSO session 0158 dates COLH67 to November 1959 and the original K. 467 issue, HMV DB3099–3102, to November 1937. This movement originally occupied DB3099 and DB3100.
carrier.matrixTakeSides.value: Probable original-side lineage: 2EA 4604-1, 2EA 4605-1, 2EA 4606-1 and 2EA 4607-2A; first movement parts 1–4 on HMV DB3099–3100.
carrier.matrixTakeSides.note: Those issued matrix/take numbers are explicitly documented by Bolig and the Schnabel chronology. Their survival in this particular Angel LP transfer is inferred, not established by runout inspection or take comparison. The LP’s own matrix/runout and pressing are unknown. No original side-join timestamps are assigned. A targeted DAHR search produced no directly usable session record, so no DAHR matrix entry is claimed.
transfer.credits.value: Bob Varney
transfer.credits.note: The source expressly states ‘Transfer by Bob Varney’; this credit is not inferred from the uploader account.
transfer.date.note: The item was added on 19 April 2010, and the current MP3 has a later file timestamp following the documented correction. Neither is an identified analogue-to-digital transfer date.
transfer.processing.note: The source identifies a mono LP transfer but gives no cartridge, equalisation, noise-reduction, editing or speed-correction procedure. Internet Archive labels the uploaded file VBR MP3 and original; ‘original’ here means the uploaded file, not an original session master.
digital.format: Internet Archive original-upload VBR MP3; documented source carrier: mono LP. Duration is the analysed file length, rounded to one decimal place.
rights.composition.value: Mozart’s concerto is public domain under the ordinary life-plus-70 term; Schnabel’s own cadenza is also beyond that term.
rights.composition.note: Mozart died in 1791; the consulted score derives from the 1878 Breitkopf edition. Schnabel died in 1951, giving an ordinary life-plus-70 expiry at the end of 2021 for his authorship. This is a territorial term calculation, not clearance of every modern edition or a claim about US cadenza publication history.
rights.recording.value: territorial — EU public-domain basis: first published in November 1937 on HMV DB3099–3102.
rights.recording.note: The LSO discography documents publication before 1963, independently of the 1937 session date. The ordinary EU 50-year sound-recording term had expired before the 2013 extension, which applies to recordings still protected at that date. This package uses that territorial basis only. US public-domain status is not established: this is not a recording first published by 1925. The Archive uploader links http://creativecommons.org/licenses/publicdomain/, but that declaration does not independently establish authority to release the performers’ or producer’s rights worldwide. The linked legal URL below is the term basis, not a Creative Commons grant.

title: Piano Concerto No. 21 in C major, K. 467
work.title: Piano Concerto No. 21 in C major
work.version.note: The performing edition is not identified. The Schnabel chronology credits his cadenzas for K. 467; the consulted orchestral score shows the finale’s cadenza slot but not the performed cadenza text. No internal cadenza themes or exact bar alignment are asserted. The Archive states that the former file mix-up with K. 595 has been corrected; attribution here follows the corrected item, without claiming independent aural authentication.
performers.note: The item, source LP sleeve and LSO discography identify the same performers. Bolig identifies the piano as a Bechstein. The honorific Sir belongs to the later source wording and is not used to date Sargent’s knighthood.
session.date.note: The LSO register dates K. 467 to 12 January 1937, separately from K. 459 on 9 and 12 January. Both finale matrix entries carry 12 January in the side-level discographies.
session.place.note: The Archive names Abbey Road Studios; the LSO, Bolig and Schnabel records specify Studio 1.
carrier.label.value: Angel Records — Great Recordings of the Century
carrier.label.note: Angel is the label of the mono LP explicitly identified as the transfer source. The original 1937 issue was on His Master’s Voice.
carrier.catalogue.note: The catalogue number appears on the photographed cover. The LSO discography dates this LP reissue to November 1959 and the complete original HMV set DB3099–3102 to November 1937. The finale occupied the two sides of DB3102.
carrier.matrixTakeSides.value: Probable original-side lineage: 2EA 4610-2A and 2EA 4611-2A; finale parts 1–2 on HMV DB3102, concerto sides 7–8.
carrier.matrixTakeSides.note: These are documented issued takes in Bolig and the Schnabel chronology; their presence in the particular Angel LP transfer is inferred rather than established by runout inspection or take comparison. The LP pressing and its own matrix/runout are unknown. No original side-join timestamp is claimed. A targeted DAHR search did not produce a usable session record, so no DAHR matrix entry is cited.
transfer.credits.value: Bob Varney
transfer.credits.note: The item explicitly states ‘Transfer by Bob Varney’, separately from its uploader metadata.
transfer.date.note: The item’s 19 April 2010 added date and the current file’s later timestamp do not identify when the LP was digitised. The correction notice is not a dated transfer log.
transfer.processing.note: No playback equipment, equalisation, denoising, editing or speed-correction procedure is supplied. The VBR MP3 original-upload descriptor identifies the digital submission, not a session master or an unprocessed transfer.
digital.format: Internet Archive original-upload VBR MP3; documented source carrier: mono LP. Duration is the analysed file length, rounded to one decimal place.
rights.composition.value: Mozart’s concerto, and Schnabel’s authorship of the credited cadenzas, are beyond the ordinary life-plus-70 term.
rights.composition.note: Mozart died in 1791 and Schnabel in 1951. Under the ordinary life-plus-70 calculation, Schnabel’s authorship term ended in 2021. The consulted orchestral score derives from the public-domain 1878 edition. This is not worldwide clearance of unidentified editorial material or a conclusion about US cadenza publication history.
rights.recording.value: territorial — EU public-domain basis: first published in November 1937 on HMV DB3099–3102.
rights.recording.note: The LSO discography expressly documents the 1937 publication, rather than merely the recording session. Its ordinary EU 50-year recording term had expired before the 2013 extension, which applies to recordings still protected at that date. The package relies on this territorial basis only. US status is not established, and the recording does not meet the publication-by-1925 cutoff. The uploader’s http://creativecommons.org/licenses/publicdomain/ declaration is recorded as source metadata, not independent proof of authority to release the performers’ or producer’s rights worldwide. The legal URL below is the term basis, not a Creative Commons grant.

title: Requiem in D minor, K. 626
work.title: Requiem in D minor, K. 626
work.version.value: Traditional Süssmayr Communio, adapting Mozart’s Introitus and Kyrie; performing edition and Walter’s alterations unidentified.
work.version.note: The NMA labels the movement Süssmayr after Mozart’s Introitus and Kyrie. This is not an independently completed final movement in Mozart’s surviving manuscript. Süssmayr’s 1800 letter explains reuse of the Kyrie fugue; Constanze’s reported instruction from Mozart is testimony, not independent verification of a complete plan. File duration includes a retained live-recording tail after the estimated musical close.
performers.note: Lisa della Casa is the soprano soloist for this movement. Commons and Internet Archive name the Wiener Staatsopernchor; the festival catalogue uses Konzertvereinigung Wiener Staatsopernchor. The primary concert archive confirms Walter, the orchestra, all four concert soloists and Franz Sauer, but leaves its choir field blank. Ira Malaniuk, Anton Dermota and Cesare Siepi belong to the full concert cast, not to an invented solo entrance in this movement.
session.date.note: The primary concert archive identifies Thursday 26 July 1956; Commons, Internet Archive and the discography agree. This is the live performance date, not the date of first publication, a later commercial issue, digitisation or upload.
session.place.value: Small Festival Hall (Kleines Festspielhaus), Salzburg, Austria
session.place.note: The Vienna Philharmonic event archive supplies Small Festival Hall. Internet Archive calls the source a live Salzburg Festival performance; the discography uses the broader Festspielhaus designation. No studio session, microphone layout or original recording medium is inferred.
carrier.label.note: The carrier actually used for this upload is unidentified. The discography lists Cetra, Nuova Era, Seven Seas and Orfeo issues of this performance. The official festival catalogue documents an Orfeo CD in 1996, but neither source ties that issue to the Ogg. A known issue is not a demonstrated transfer source.
carrier.catalogue.note: No catalogue number is attached to the transferred source. Cetra LO516, Nuova Era 2209, Seven Seas K30Y307 and Orfeo C430961B are documented release leads only. The festival catalogue dates Orfeo C 430 961 B to 1996; that is not evidence of first release or byte provenance.
carrier.matrixTakeSides.note: No matrix, take or side identifiers are supplied for the source used. The file is a complete movement from a live performance; neither a shellac carrier nor an original tape generation is established. No physical side join is assigned to a musical event.
transfer.credits.note: D. Benjamin Miller is the Commons uploader, not an established transfer or mastering engineer. The Internet Archive uploader/scanner fields document repository submission, not who digitised, edited or restored the recording. No transfer-engineer credit has been found.
transfer.date.note: Internet Archive added/public date is 4 June 2018; Commons upload is 5 June 2018. These are not transfer dates. The embedded Commons digitizing year 1956 duplicates the performance year without a transfer history and is not accepted as such evidence. The 1996 Orfeo issue is also not assigned as the date of this transfer.
transfer.processing.value: Internet Archive lists the corresponding Ogg Vorbis movement file as an original upload; Commons supplies Ogg Vorbis and an MP3 access derivative.
transfer.processing.note: Here original means the repository’s uploaded file, not an original session master. The chain from the unidentified physical or broadcast source to the Ogg is undocumented. Session medium, tape generation, speed correction, equalisation, noise reduction, editing and restoration settings remain unknown; no such processing is inferred from the transfer’s sound.
digital.format: MP3 access derivative supplied by Wikimedia Commons; uploaded source: Ogg Vorbis; complete movement with retained live-recording tail
rights.composition.value: Underlying Mozart–Süssmayr composition is out of copyright where the ordinary life-plus-70 term applies.
rights.composition.note: Mozart died in 1791 and Süssmayr in 1803; the traditional full score was published in 1800. This is a term-based assessment of the historical composition, not a worldwide clearance, a licence for a modern critical edition, or evidence about the sound recording.
rights.recording.value: Rule 1 — territorial recording claim: Commons applies PD-EU-audio; upstream Internet Archive applies Public Domain Mark 1.0.
rights.recording.note: The documented fact is the sources’ sound-recording rights assertion. PD-EU-audio is territorial: US status is not established, and no worldwide clearance is claimed. Public Domain Mark is not CC0 or a performer’s licence. The 1956 performance date does not prove first lawful publication or communication before 1963; that history is unestablished. The known 1996 Orfeo issue and 2018 uploads are not substituted for it. Admission therefore uses the explicit Commons PD-EU-audio route, not a calculated pre-1963-publication claim.

title: Requiem in D minor, K. 626
work.title: Requiem in D minor, K. 626
work.version.value: Traditional Mozart–Süssmayr completion, Dies irae; performing edition and Walter’s alterations unidentified.
work.version.note: Mozart left the vocal and bass framework and some instrumental indications; the traditional completed orchestration is used as the reference. The recording sources do not name a printed edition. The NMA preface quotes Walter’s policy of cutting some trombone doublings, but does not map it to this 1956 performance. The complete movement includes its orchestral postlude.
performers.note: This movement is for chorus, without a solo vocal part; the concert’s vocal solo quartet is not credited as singing here. Commons and Internet Archive name the Wiener Staatsopernchor; the festival catalogue uses Konzertvereinigung Wiener Staatsopernchor. The primary concert archive confirms Walter, the orchestra, all four concert soloists and Franz Sauer, but leaves its choir field blank. Ira Malaniuk, Anton Dermota and Cesare Siepi belong to the full concert cast, not to an invented solo entrance in this movement.
session.date.note: The primary concert archive identifies Thursday 26 July 1956; Commons, Internet Archive and the discography agree. This is the live performance date, not the date of first publication, a later commercial issue, digitisation or upload.
session.place.value: Small Festival Hall (Kleines Festspielhaus), Salzburg, Austria
session.place.note: The Vienna Philharmonic event archive supplies Small Festival Hall. Internet Archive calls the source a live Salzburg Festival performance; the discography uses the broader Festspielhaus designation. No studio session, microphone layout or original recording medium is inferred.
carrier.label.note: The carrier actually used for this upload is unidentified. The discography lists Cetra, Nuova Era, Seven Seas and Orfeo issues of this performance. The official festival catalogue documents an Orfeo CD in 1996, but neither source ties that issue to the Ogg. A known issue is not a demonstrated transfer source.
carrier.catalogue.note: No catalogue number is attached to the transferred source. Cetra LO516, Nuova Era 2209, Seven Seas K30Y307 and Orfeo C430961B are documented release leads only. The festival catalogue dates Orfeo C 430 961 B to 1996; that is not evidence of first release or byte provenance.
carrier.matrixTakeSides.note: No matrix, take or side identifiers are supplied for the source used. The file is a complete movement from a live performance; neither a shellac carrier nor an original tape generation is established. No physical side join is assigned to a musical event.
transfer.credits.note: D. Benjamin Miller is the Commons uploader, not an established transfer or mastering engineer. The Internet Archive uploader/scanner fields document repository submission, not who digitised, edited or restored the recording. No transfer-engineer credit has been found.
transfer.date.note: Internet Archive added/public date is 4 June 2018; Commons upload is 5 June 2018. These are not transfer dates. The embedded Commons digitizing year 1956 duplicates the performance year without a transfer history and is not accepted as such evidence. The 1996 Orfeo issue is also not assigned as the date of this transfer.
transfer.processing.value: Internet Archive lists the corresponding Ogg Vorbis movement file as an original upload; Commons supplies Ogg Vorbis and an MP3 access derivative.
transfer.processing.note: Here original means the repository’s uploaded file, not an original session master. The chain from the unidentified physical or broadcast source to the Ogg is undocumented. Session medium, tape generation, speed correction, equalisation, noise reduction, editing and restoration settings remain unknown; no such processing is inferred from the transfer’s sound.
digital.format: MP3 access derivative supplied by Wikimedia Commons; uploaded source: Ogg Vorbis; complete movement
rights.composition.value: Underlying Mozart–Süssmayr composition is out of copyright where the ordinary life-plus-70 term applies.
rights.composition.note: Mozart died in 1791 and Süssmayr in 1803; the traditional full score was published in 1800. This is a term-based assessment of the historical composition, not a worldwide clearance, a licence for a modern critical edition, or evidence about the sound recording.
rights.recording.value: Rule 1 — territorial recording claim: Commons applies PD-EU-audio; upstream Internet Archive applies Public Domain Mark 1.0.
rights.recording.note: The documented fact is the sources’ sound-recording rights assertion. PD-EU-audio is territorial: US status is not established, and no worldwide clearance is claimed. Public Domain Mark is not CC0 or a performer’s licence. The 1956 performance date does not prove first lawful publication or communication before 1963; that history is unestablished. The known 1996 Orfeo issue and 2018 uploads are not substituted for it. Admission therefore uses the explicit Commons PD-EU-audio route, not a calculated pre-1963-publication claim.

work.title: Mille regretz
work.catalogue: NJE 28.25; attributed to Josquin des Prez
work.version.value: Four-part unaccompanied vocal chanson; exact performing edition unknown
work.version.note: The inspected Smijers score has superius, contratenor, tenor and bassus, 41 bars. It supports texture and scoring, not a claim that this choir used that edition, its spelling or its pitch level.
work.authorship.value: Traditionally attributed to Josquin des Prez; attribution disputed
work.authorship.note: The traditional name is retained as a qualified attribution, not a settled authorship claim. IMSLP notes modern dispute and David Fallows’s defence of Josquin; Commons’s unqualified composer label is insufficient to settle the issue.

title: Douce dame jolie / L’espoir que j’ai
movement: Machaut and Janequin · Weckerlin arrangements · complete Victor side
work.title: Douce dame jolie / L’espoir que j’ai
work.movement: Complete paired Victor side: Machaut and Janequin in later arrangements
work.version.value: Two songs from J.-B. Weckerlin’s Échos du temps passé, volume I, performed with harp and lute
work.version.note: The label numbers Machaut’s Douce dame jolie first and Janequin’s L’espoir que j’ai second; DAHR quotes the collection title and volume from Victor’s ledgers. BnF describes the published collection as voice with piano, so the precise harp-and-lute adaptation is not established from that score.
work.date.value: Fourteenth- and sixteenth-century songs; nineteenth-century published arrangement collection
work.date.note: The label prints 1350 A.D. and 1530 A.D. as historical song dates; these are retained only as label assertions, not verified composition dates. BnF dates volume I to 1853–1857.
work.completeness.value: Entire published two-song acoustic side; not a complete original Machaut virelai
work.completeness.note: No digital mid-phrase extract is made. Original stanza completeness and the exact boundary between the two arranged songs are unestablished; the side remains one authored section.
performers.note: DAHR identifies Raymond Dixon as Murphy’s pseudonym, not a second singer. Di Stefano is credited for takes 3–4; Francis J. Lapitino belongs only to discarded takes 1–2 and is not credited on this issued take.
session.date.note: Take 4 was made on 17 March 1915. The earlier matrix date 14 January 1915 refers to destroyed takes 1–2, not the recording streamed here.
session.place.value: New York, New York, United States
session.place.note: DAHR specifies New York for takes 3–4. Camden belongs to the January takes and is not substituted for this session; the studio address is unknown.
carrier.label.value: Victor Talking Machine Company; blue label
carrier.label.note: The viewed label names Victor and Lambert Murphy and specifies tenor with harp and lute, in French.
carrier.catalogue.note: The side suffix B is visible on the label. LOC and DAHR identify the 10-inch carrier.
carrier.matrixTakeSides.note: DAHR marks take 4 as Master and links the same audio. Matrix/take identification comes from discographic records, not from claiming to read an illegible run-out inscription.
carrier.publication.note: Bolig’s entry 45083 gives May-16 as release date. This corrects the Archive mirror’s claim of first publication in 1915, which conflates release with the session year.
transfer.credits.value: Source disc: UCSB Davidson Library, Department of Special Collections; National Jukebox digital access; Hessel Digital Library mirror
transfer.credits.note: LOC identifies the source collection. The mirror credits digitisation to the Library of Congress Packard Campus; DAHR also describes the audio as from the UCSB Library. No individual transfer engineer is established.
transfer.date.note: The original disc-transfer date is unknown. The Archive mirror states LOC retrieval on 30 September 2026 and repository publication on 10 October 2026; neither is the 1915 session or 1916 release.
transfer.processing.value: Archive describes its MP3 as a bit-exact copy of the LOC-served MP3, with no processing
transfer.processing.note: This records the mirror’s provenance statement, not an independently performed checksum comparison. Original stylus, speed correction, equalisation and noise-reduction settings are unknown. No additional audio cut is made.
digital.format: MP3 mirror of the complete National Jukebox side
rights.composition.value: Historical songs and Weckerlin collection are outside ordinary composition copyright terms
rights.composition.note: BnF gives Weckerlin’s dates 1821–1910 and the collection’s publication in 1853–1857. The exact person responsible for adapting its piano accompaniment to harp and lute is not established. Recording admission rests independently on the documented pre-cutoff publication.
rights.recording.value: Rule 2 — United States public domain: published May 1916
rights.recording.note: Victor 45083’s documented 1916 publication precedes the project’s 1925 cutoff. source.rights uses us-published-before-cutoff with published 1916. The Archive Public Domain Mark is corroborative, not the sole basis; its 1915 first-publication claim and simplified statutory explanation are not repeated. This is a US basis, not a claim of worldwide clearance.
rights.creditLine: Machaut, Douce dame jolie, and Janequin, L’espoir que j’ai, from Weckerlin’s Échos du temps passé; Lambert Murphy, tenor, Stefano Di Stefano, harp, William Carlino, lute. Recorded New York, 17 March 1915; Victor 45083-B, matrix B-15595, take 4; released May 1916. Source disc UCSB; Library of Congress, National Jukebox; Hessel Digital Library mirror on Internet Archive. US public-domain recording.

title: Quel augellin che canta
work.title: Quel augellin che canta
work.version.value: Five-part unaccompanied vocal setting, SSATB
work.version.note: The opened score supplies two soprano, alto, tenor and bass parts, without instruments. Neither the exact edition used by the choir nor its performance transposition is established.
work.publication.note: Publication date, not a guessed composition year.
work.text.value: Giovanni Battista Guarini, adapted from Il pastor fido, Act I, scene 1
work.text.note: LiederNet identifies lines 175–186 and distinguishes Monteverdi’s adapted text. Public prose paraphrases the imagery; no copyrighted modern translation or exact timed syllable is supplied.
work.completeness.value: Whole nominated Tudor Consort madrigal track
work.completeness.note: The published concert track is retained intact, including its quiet tail. It is not grouped as a multi-movement set merely because it appears in Book IV or on an album.
work.scoreEdition.value: Daniel Van Gilst, 2019, CC0, four-page SSATB score
work.scoreEdition.note: The complete score was opened and viewed. This modern engraving is dedicated to the public domain under CC0. Its transposition is not used to identify the choir’s sounding key or pitch standard.
performers.note: The track description and Carey’s album notes agree. Five written parts do not establish five individual singers, and no instrumental players are credited.
session.date.note: The track names the Ordizia concert; the album’s first-person liner notes explicitly date it to Wednesday 2 November 2005. The 19 August 2010 date on FMA and Commons is an online release, not the recording session.
session.place.note: The track and album notes name the venue. The later Rome concert and 2006 New Zealand recording described elsewhere in the same album notes belong to different tracks.
carrier.label.note: The album was prepared for the Tudor Consort’s twentieth anniversary, but no original imprint is named. FMA and Commons are access repositories.
carrier.catalogue.note: No commercial catalogue number is supplied.
carrier.matrixTakeSides.note: The notes refer to a disc but supply no matrix, mastering identifier or take number.
carrier.album.note: A mixed concert anthology, with different sessions explicitly distinguished in the liner notes.
transfer.credits.value: Timothy Hurd, producer and engineer; Commons import by ComputerHotline
transfer.credits.note: Hurd is explicitly credited at album level. The Commons uploader is not presented as the original engineer.
transfer.date.note: The 2005 concert date, 2010 FMA release and 11 April 2020 Commons upload do not establish a mastering or transfer date.
transfer.processing.value: FMA MP3 source converted to Ogg for Commons; Wikimedia MP3 access derivative
transfer.processing.note: Original recording medium, microphones, editing and equalisation settings are not supplied. No further processing or audio trim is introduced here.
digital.format: MP3 access derivative of the Commons Ogg import from FMA
rights.composition.value: Public-domain 1603 madrigal; inspected engraving dedicated under CC0
rights.composition.note: Historical composition rights and Van Gilst’s engraving status are separate from the Tudor Consort’s sound recording rights.
rights.recording.value: Rule 1 — CC BY 3.0 Unported
rights.recording.note: The external FMA track was opened directly and explicitly licenses this human choral performance under CC BY 3.0, without a NonCommercial condition. Commons contains a 2024 review template referring anomalously to a Flickr image; that text is not relied upon as verification of an FMA recording. The actual FMA recording page supplies independent evidence.

title: Sicut lilium inter spinas
work.title: Sicut lilium inter spinas
work.version.value: Unaccompanied motet for cantus, altus, tenor, second tenor and bassus
work.version.note: The five-part score is the motet, not the Mass of the same name. The album lists the motet as track 1 and the Mass movements separately. The choir’s exact performing edition and pitch are not identified.
work.publication.note: 1569 is publication, not an asserted exact composition year. Suggestions that it may be an early work are not converted into a date.
work.text.value: Song of Songs, beginning with the lily among thorns comparison, followed by Alleluia
work.text.note: The text is described as a whole; no line is assigned an exact timestamp without alignment.
work.completeness.note: No Mass movement is appended, and no editorial audio excerpt is made.
work.scoreEdition.value: Theodor de Witt, Palestrina’s Werke, volume I, Leipzig: Breitkopf & Härtel, 1862, plate 10414
work.scoreEdition.note: Public-domain edition. Motet No. 21 spans printed pp. 90–94, PDF pp. 104–108; those pages were opened and viewed, including the final cadence on p. 94.
performers.note: These are credits for the nominated recording, not the separate Hyperion performances consulted for programme notes. Individual singers and choir size are not identified.
session.date.note: FMA describes a live minidisc recording and gives the album date as 29 July 2007. The choir’s own archive documents the matching Renaissance Influences programme on that date. Their conjunction supports a probable session date, but the track description does not explicitly identify the session day. The FMA track’s 20 August 2010 is its online release.
session.place.value: Sacred Heart Cathedral, Hill Street, Wellington, New Zealand
session.place.note: The official archive supplies the venue for the matching 29 July 2007 concert. The link between that concert and the recording is inferred from title, director, programme and album date, not stated in the track description.
carrier.label.note: No original recording label or commercial imprint is named; Free Music Archive is the distribution platform.
carrier.catalogue.note: The album title and track number are known, but no release catalogue number is supplied.
carrier.matrixTakeSides.note: The source describes a live minidisc recording, not a pressed disc matrix; no session take number is supplied.
carrier.album.value: Renaissance influences — Pizzetti: Messa di Requiem / Palestrina: Missa Sicut lilium inter spinas, track 1
carrier.album.note: The motet remains an independently authored recording here; the album is not turned into a multi-movement set.
transfer.credits.value: Commons import from FMA by ComputerHotline
transfer.credits.note: The recording or minidisc-transfer engineer is not named. The uploader credit does not imply that ComputerHotline made the original recording.
transfer.date.note: The online track release is 20 August 2010; the Commons upload is 11 April 2020. No separate minidisc transfer or mastering date is established.
transfer.processing.value: Live minidisc source; FMA MP3 converted to Ogg for Commons, with Wikimedia MP3 access derivative
transfer.processing.note: The source format chain is described by the album and Commons source entry. Microphone placement, equalisation, noise reduction and any earlier editing are unknown. No additional trim by Contrapunctus.

rights.composition.note: The 1569 work and public-domain 1862 score are distinct from the Tudor Consort’s modern performance rights.

title: Barcarolle, Op. 10 No. 3
work.title: Barcarolle
work.version.value: Solo piano, performed by the composer
work.version.note: No performing score edition is identified, and the printed text is not asserted to match the performance.
session.date.note: Sources agree on April 1919 and disagree on the day. The Archive filenames, the RCA register and the Library of Congress bulletin give 23 April; DAHR’s Edison ledger entry and the Classical Pianists chronology give 24 April. The day is not resolved here.
session.place.note: DAHR gives New York for every take. The Library of Congress bulletin names Edison Studios, New York. The label place of publication, Orange, New Jersey, is not the session place.
carrier.label.note: Edison is the original label (released at Orange, New Jersey, according to DAHR’s label record); the uploader identifies the 1992 RCA/BMG set as the immediate source of the file.
carrier.catalogue.value: Edison Diamond Disc 82202 (10-inch double-faced; Barcarolle on side L, Chopin’s Valse in A♭, Op. 64 No. 3, on side R); RCA-BMG 09026 61265 2, CD 10 (1992)
carrier.catalogue.note: The side assignment and disc number are documented by the Edison list and the Library of Congress bulletin; the disc used for the 1992 transfer is not identified. DAHR’s MARC record for the disc gives 10-inch, 80 rpm and a bracketed publication year of [1919], which predates the release documented by Densmore (February 1921) and by the Library of Congress ([1921]) and is not followed for the release date; either year is before 1926.
carrier.matrixTakeSides.note: The RCA register names Edison 6743-C for CD 10, track 16, and the Archive file is that track. Edison issued all three takes (A, B, C) on the same catalogue number, so the disc number alone does not identify the take, and no comparison of takes was made. DAHR gives its own take dates (24 April 1919) which differ from the RCA register (23 April).
transfer.credits.value: John Pfeiffer, reissue producer; Ward Marston, disc-to-DAT transfer; André Gauthier, remastering supervisor; Anthony Salvatore, remastering engineer
transfer.credits.note: These are the credits printed for the 1992 RCA/BMG set. Their connection to this access file rests on the uploader’s identification of the item as CD 10 of that set. The later ripper and uploader are not named as engineers.
transfer.date.note: The set was issued in 1992, but the dates of the disc-to-DAT transfer, the remastering and the later CD extraction are not stated. The Internet Archive upload of 11 October 2025 is not a transfer date.
transfer.processing.value: Disc-to-DAT transfer, then digital remastering at BMG/RCA Studios, New York City; the Internet Archive derives its VBR MP3 from an uploaded WAV.
transfer.processing.note: The booklet says surface imperfections were reduced without radical removal of all surface noise. It gives no equalisation, pitch-correction, noise-reduction or editing settings, and none is inferred from the audio analysis. The booklet’s essay says the Edison engineer evidently placed the upright piano too far from the recording horns, so the sound is distant.
digital.format: VBR MP3 access derivative; the uploaded source is a WAV taken from a 1992 CD reissue of an acoustic disc
rights.composition.value: Underlying composition is out of copyright where the ordinary life-plus-70 term applies.
rights.composition.note: Rachmaninoff died in 1943. This is a territorial term calculation, not worldwide clearance or a statement about any modern edition.
rights.recording.value: US public domain: the issued sound recording was published by 1925 (Edison Diamond Disc 82202, released February 1921).
rights.recording.note: Densmore’s Edison list gives a February 1921 release for 82202, and the Library of Congress Cataloging Service Bulletin 61 catalogues the disc as Edison [1921]; this is independent of the April 1919 session date. The Archive item’s Public Domain Mark is noted but not relied on. The 1992 booklet carries an all-rights-reserved reissue notice: no claim is made that its text, artwork or compilation is public domain, or that any new creative contribution to the mastering is cleared worldwide.

work.title: Piano Concerto No. 2 in C minor
work.movement: II. Adagio sostenuto — opening 78-rpm side only
work.version.note: The performing edition is not identified. This file is the complete transfer of the slow movement’s first original side, part 4 of the concerto’s disc sequence. It omits the subsequent sides, including the later central section, cadenza and return; no sides have been joined.
performers.note: The HMV label uses Philadelphia Symphony Orchestra; DAHR identifies the ensemble as the Philadelphia Orchestra.
session.date.note: DAHR identifies take 1 as the issued master. The Archive’s November 1929 date describes the HMV issue, not the recording session.
session.place.note: The matrix’s Take Date and Place table names the Academy of Music. Camden in the issue’s MARC publisher imprint is not adopted as a recording venue.
carrier.label.value: His Master’s Voice / The Gramophone Co. Ltd.
carrier.label.note: UK 12-inch 78-rpm pressing, manufactured at Hayes, Middlesex, England according to the label.
carrier.catalogue.note: The label marks the side No. 4 and 2nd Movement–Adagio sostenuto (1st Record). The other face contains the first movement’s third side. Internet Archive dates the HMV issue to November 1929; DAHR’s generated MARC imprint gives [1929].
carrier.matrixTakeSides.value: Victor CVE-48966, take 1; Gramophone face number 2-05744; concerto part 4
carrier.matrixTakeSides.note: DAHR connects the master take to DB-1334 and distinguishes 2-05744 as a Gramophone face number. The Archive transcribes A48966 as another disc identifier; it is not treated as a separate performance or take.
transfer.credits.value: Phoebe Pugh, transfer and metadata; Akin Gaddis, disc cleaning; George Blood, L.P., digitisation
transfer.credits.note: Credits are the Archive’s user_transferred, user_metadataentered, user_cleaned and scanningcenter fields. The carrier belongs to the Leif Druedahl collection.
transfer.date.note: The item was made public on 20 April 2023; this is an upload date, not a documented transfer date.
transfer.processing.value: Digitised at 78 rpm; preferred 3.3-mil truncated-conical stylus transfer, equalised with turnover 500.0; 24-bit FLAC master and VBR MP3 access derivative.
transfer.processing.note: The Archive documents four stylus transfers and identifies the chosen stylus in the preferred FLAC comment. No additional restoration or speed correction has been applied for this edition. Surface noise limits automatic onset and pitch-class estimates; these are not treated as counts of played notes or verified changes of key.
digital.format: VBR MP3 derivative of the George Blood 24-bit FLAC transfer; one original 78-rpm side, unjoined
rights.composition.value: Public domain in ordinary life-plus-70 jurisdictions.
rights.composition.note: Rachmaninoff died on 28 March 1943. This concerns the composition, not the separately assessed recording, transfer or an unidentified modern edition.
rights.recording.value: Territorial EU public-domain basis: sound recording published before 1963.
rights.recording.note: Rule 3. Internet Archive dates HMV DB-1334 to November 1929, and DAHR’s issue record supplies a [1929] publication imprint and the link to CVE-48966 take 1. The former 50-year recording term expired before the 2013 extension, which applies to recordings still protected on 1 November 2013. US public-domain status is not established. This independent George Blood transfer has no licenceurl or non-commercial condition in the consulted item metadata and identifies its own original FLAC and physical carrier. F. Reeder’s separate RACHMANINOFFPianoConcertoNo.2InCMinor-NEWTRANSFER carries CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 and is expressly excluded, not an upstream source for this audio. This is a territorial recording-term assessment, not a worldwide licence or a claim that the modern transfer has been freely licensed.

work.version.note: The performing edition, revision and any editorial interventions are not identified in the consulted recording documentation.
session.date.note: Commons gives 1 January 1959, but the embedded tag gives only the year. The dated 9/59 sleeve is a release-carrier date, not a session date. No day or month is adopted without session documentation.
session.place.note: The original issue identifies the recording collaboration with Polskie Nagrania in Warsaw; a particular hall is not documented in this source.
carrier.catalogue.note: Documented original stereo issue. The precise LP, CD or digital edition copied into the Commons FLAC is unknown.
carrier.matrixTakeSides.note: No matrix, take or side information is established. A digital file alone does not establish that no earlier physical carrier existed.
transfer.credits.note: The original recording credits name Heinz Wildhagen (recording engineer) and Hans Weber (recording supervisor). They are not documented as the transfer or restoration staff for this FLAC.
transfer.date.note: No transfer date is documented; upload and encoding-software dates are not session or transfer dates.
transfer.processing.value: Embedded encoder: libFLAC 1.3.2 20170101. Commons master: FLAC, 16-bit, 44.1 kHz, 2 channels.
transfer.processing.note: These are file properties, not evidence of noise reduction, equalisation, pitch correction or other restoration. Earlier processing is not documented.
digital.format: MP3 access derivative; Commons master: FLAC, 16-bit, 44.1 kHz, 2 channels
rights.composition.value: Original composition is public domain in ordinary life-plus-70 jurisdictions.

work.version.note: The performing edition is not identified. This file is the complete transfer of the first original side, not a complete movement and not a reconstruction from joined sides. The HMV label calls the movement Allegro moderato; DAHR gives Moderato.
performers.note: The HMV label uses Philadelphia Symphony Orchestra; DAHR identifies the ensemble as the Philadelphia Orchestra.
session.date.note: DAHR identifies take 3 as the issued master. The Archive’s 1930 date describes the issued record, not this session.
session.place.note: The matrix’s Take Date and Place table names the Academy of Music. Camden in the issue’s MARC publisher imprint is not adopted as a recording venue.
carrier.label.value: His Master’s Voice / The Gramophone Co. Ltd.
carrier.label.note: UK 12-inch 78-rpm pressing, manufactured at Hayes, Middlesex, England according to the label.
carrier.catalogue.note: First side of the first movement; the label marks it No. 1 and 1st Record. Internet Archive dates the issue to 1930; DAHR’s generated MARC imprint gives [1929]. Publication was therefore documented well before 1963, without resolving the precise first issue date.
carrier.matrixTakeSides.value: Victor CVE-48963, take 3; Gramophone face number 42-600; concerto part 1
carrier.matrixTakeSides.note: DAHR connects the master take to DB-1333 and distinguishes 42-600 as a Gramophone face number. The Archive transcribes A48963 as another disc identifier; it is not treated as a separate performance or take.
transfer.credits.value: Phoebe Pugh, transfer and metadata; Akin Gaddis, disc cleaning; George Blood, L.P., digitisation
transfer.credits.note: Credits are the Archive’s user_transferred, user_metadataentered, user_cleaned and scanningcenter fields. The carrier belongs to the Leif Druedahl collection.
transfer.date.note: The item was made public on 19 April 2023; this is an upload date, not a documented transfer date.
transfer.processing.value: Digitised at 78 rpm; preferred 3.3-mil truncated-conical stylus transfer, equalised with turnover 500.0; 24-bit FLAC master and VBR MP3 access derivative.
transfer.processing.note: The Archive documents four stylus transfers and identifies the chosen stylus in the preferred FLAC comment. Technical notes report minor distortion and some wow/pitch warble. No additional restoration or speed correction has been applied for this edition; measured pitch-class or attack estimates must not be read as reliable tuning or ornament counts.
digital.format: VBR MP3 derivative of the George Blood 24-bit FLAC transfer; one original 78-rpm side, unjoined
rights.composition.value: Public domain in ordinary life-plus-70 jurisdictions.
rights.composition.note: Rachmaninoff died on 28 March 1943. This concerns the composition, not the separately assessed recording, transfer or an unidentified modern edition.
rights.recording.value: Territorial EU public-domain basis: sound recording published before 1963.
rights.recording.note: Rule 3. The HMV DB-1333 issue is dated 1930 by the Archive and [1929] in DAHR’s MARC imprint; 1930 is the conservative documented publication bound used in source.rights. Its former 50-year recording term expired before the 2013 extension, which applies to recordings still protected on 1 November 2013. US public-domain status is not established. This independent George Blood transfer has no licenceurl or non-commercial condition in the consulted item metadata and identifies its own original FLAC and physical carrier. F. Reeder’s separate RACHMANINOFFPianoConcertoNo.2InCMinor-NEWTRANSFER carries CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 and is expressly excluded, not an upstream source for this audio. This is a territorial recording-term assessment, not a worldwide licence or a claim that the modern transfer has been freely licensed.
